newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: New date set for inauguration of Angolan government.
newsitem.headline: New date set for inauguration of Angolan government.

text.p: After weeks of delay, the Angola government and the former UNITA rebels have set March 20 as a new date to establish a national unity government, the United Nations reported on Wednesday.

The decision by the two parties who fought each other for decades since independence from Portugal came after the U.N. Security Council put pressure on UNITA to comply by threatening to close down the U.N. peacekeeping operation if no progress was made.

The formation of a new government, originally scheduled for Jan. 25, was postponed several times, mainly because of problems in finding an acceptable role for UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi, who still controls much of Angola.
The latest agreement on a timetable was concluded at a meeting of the Joint Commission on Monday and Tuesday in the Angolan capital of Luanda, spokesman Juan Carlos Brandt said.
Deputies from UNITA are expected to take their seats in a new National Assembly by March 18 and "the government of National Unity and Reconciliation should be inaugurated on March 20," Brandt said.

The meeting also set a new timetable for the selection and incorporation of some UNITA soldiers into the Angolan armed forces and demobilization of others. The selection process is supposed to be completed by March 10, and demobilization is to begin on March 15.

U.N. military commanders at the meeting said the number of deserters from areas where UNITA troops had assembled now numbered 26,407 and needed to be reduced, officials said. They urged the government to allocate the funds necessary for the men who were to be demobilized.

The United Nations has 6,638 troops, military observers and civilian police from more than 30 countries in Angola. It is helping to implement a peace agreement signed in Lusaka, Zambia, in November 1994 which ended the civil war.

On Feb. 26, the U.N. Security Council in New York adopted a resolution blaming former UNITA rebels for delays in establishing a national unity government in Angola. The 15-member body extended the mandate of the U.N. force there for one month only, until March 31.

The move was to enable the council to keep the situation under close scrutiny. The Council also said it was ready, in case of further delays, to impose trade sanctions on UNITA and travel restrictions on its senior officials.
